summary: Specifies conventions for using the RSA Key Encapsulation Mechanism, defined in ISO/IEC 18033-2, in the Cryptographic Message Syntax. A sender uses it to securely send keying material to a recipient using the recipient's RSA public key. It obsoletes RFC 5990.

eli5.summary: You can lock a secret code into a box that only the receiver's key opens. This explains how to use that trick inside secure messages. It replaces RFC 5990.

questions: how to use rsa-kem in cms
how does rsa-kem work in cms
subtitle: How to protect a message's encryption key with RSA-KEM, using the CMS KEMRecipientInfo structure.

tldr.problem: Senders using the Cryptographic Message Syntax need a way to deliver keying material to a recipient's RSA public key, with stronger security assurance than PKCS #1 v1.5 key transport.
tldr.mechanism: The sender encrypts a random integer with the recipient's RSA public key, derives a shared secret from it with a key derivation function, and uses that to wrap the content-encryption key inside a KEMRecipientInfo.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 5990, which used KeyTransRecipientInfo. Ciphertext and wrapped key now travel in separate fields.

today: RFC 9690 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 5990, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What RSA-KEM Is For
sections.content:
The RSA Key Encapsulation Mechanism (RSA-KEM) is a one-pass (store-and-forward) mechanism for an originator to securely send keying material to a recipient using the recipient's RSA public key. It is specified in Clause 11.5 of ISO/IEC 18033-2:2006.

It takes a different approach from other RSA key transport mechanisms such as those in RFC 8017. It encrypts a random integer with the recipient's RSA public key and derives a shared secret from that integer. Both sides can then derive a symmetric key from the shared secret, for example a key-encryption key (KEK) that wraps a content-encryption key (CEK).

This document gives the conventions for using RSA-KEM as a standalone KEM and with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) via KEMRecipientInfo from RFC 9629.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing the secret key itself, you lock a random number in a box only the receiver can open. Both of you then use that number to make the same secret key.

sections.title: The Three KEM Functions
sections.content:
Like every KEM, RSA-KEM provides KeyGen(), Encapsulate() and Decapsulate().

  • Encapsulate: given the recipient's public key, generate a random integer z between 0 and n-1, compute the ciphertext ct = z^e mod n, and derive the shared secret SS = KDF(Z, ssLen). The ciphertext goes to the recipient.
  • Decapsulate: with the private key, recover z = ct^d mod n and derive the same SS.

The random integer z MUST be generated independently at random for each encryption operation, whether for the same or different recipients. Intermediate values such as z MUST be securely deleted when no longer needed. The recipient outputs a decryption error if the received ciphertext is shorter than the modulus length or is not an integer between 0 and n-1.
sections.eli5: The sender picks a random number, locks it with the receiver's public lock, and keeps a copy. The receiver unlocks it with the private key. Now both hold the same number.

sections.title: Why RSA-KEM Gives Higher Assurance
sections.content:
The RFC gives two reasons. First, the input to the RSA operation is a string-encoded random integer, so it has no structure an adversary could exploit. Second, the input is independent of the keying material, so the result of the RSA decryption is not directly available to an adversary. As a result RSA-KEM has a tight security proof in the random oracle model. In padding schemes such as PKCS #1 v1.5 the input has structure and depends on the keying material.

It is also architecturally convenient: the public-key operations are separate from the symmetric operations on the keying material, and the length of the keying material is set by the symmetric algorithms, not by the RSA modulus size.
sections.eli5: Because the locked thing is just a random number with no pattern, there is nothing for a snooper to pick at.

sections.title: Using It in CMS KEMRecipientInfo
sections.content:
RSA-KEM MAY be used for one or more recipients of the CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data or authenticated-enveloped-data content types. The recipient's RecipientInfo MUST be OtherRecipientInfo using KEMRecipientInfo.

The originator runs Encapsulate(pk) to get (ct, SS), derives KEK = KDF(SS, kekLength, otherInfo), and wraps the CEK to get WK. The recipient reverses this with Decapsulate, the KDF and an unwrap. The KDF used for CMS MAY differ from the KDF used inside RSA-KEM.

Key field values: version MUST be 0, kem MUST contain id-kem-rsa, kemct carries the ciphertext, kdf and wrap name the algorithms, kekLength is the KEK size in octets, and encryptedKey holds the wrapped keying material.
sections.eli5: The message envelope has a slot for each reader. In each slot go the locked number and the message's real key, which has been wrapped using a key made from that number.

sections.title: Mandatory Algorithms and Certificates
sections.content:
An implementation that supports RSA-KEM MUST support at least KDF3 (from ANS X9.44) with SHA-256 as the key derivation function, and the AES-Wrap-128 key-encryption algorithm from RFC 3394. It MAY support others.

A recipient MAY identify its public key in a certificate with the plain rsaEncryption identifier, but that does not signal willingness to accept RSA-KEM. If the recipient wants the key used only with RSA-KEM, it MUST use the id-rsa-kem-spki identifier, and the parameters SHOULD be absent, in which case KDF3 with SHA-256 is used. If a keyUsage extension is present for such a key, it MUST contain only keyEncipherment.

Support can be announced with the S/MIME SMIMECapabilities attribute, using id-rsa-kem-spki in the capabilityID field. When parameters are present they use the GenericHybridParameters type, and the values given there MUST be used in the kdf, kekLength and wrap fields of KEMRecipientInfo.
sections.eli5: Everyone must at least know one standard way to stir the number into a key and one standard way to wrap the key. A certificate can say the key is only for this job.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 5990
sections.content:
RFC 5990 used RSA-KEM as a key transport algorithm with KeyTransRecipientInfo, and sent one combined EK that concatenated the ciphertext and the wrapped key. Here the ciphertext is in kemct and the wrapped key is in encryptedKey.

  • Camellia, Triple-DES and SHA-1 are no longer discussed, though their identifiers remain in the ASN.1 module.
  • KDF3 is still required, now with SHA-256 as the hash.
  • Other KDFs and key-encryption algorithms are simply allowed, not recommended.
  • Only one RSA-based KEM, identified by id-kem-rsa, is supported.
  • id-rsa-kem-spki is introduced as an alias for id-rsa-kem to avoid confusion with id-kem-rsa.
  • The new ASN.1 module produces the same bits on the wire as the one in RFC 5990.
sections.eli5: The old version sent the locked number and the wrapped key glued together. The new one puts them in separate labelled boxes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RSA-KEM should be considered as a replacement for the key transport part of PKCS #1 v1.5 in new CMS applications, to avoid potential chosen-ciphertext vulnerabilities and gain a tighter proof. The cost is slightly longer encrypted keying material.

Key size must match the desired security level. As an example, for 128-bit security the RSA key would be at least 3072 bits, the KDF would use SHA-256, and the key-encryption algorithm would be AES Key Wrap with a 128-bit key. Security depends on a quality random number generator (see RFC 4086), and implementations MUST NOT use z directly for any purpose.

Implementations SHOULD NOT leak information through timing or other side channels. An RSA key pair used for RSA-KEM SHOULD NOT also be used for digital signatures, other key establishment schemes, data encryption, or more than one set of underlying algorithm components. The same key pair may be used with both RFC 5990 and this document, because the RSA operations are identical.
sections.eli5: Use good random numbers, do not give away clues by how long you take, and keep one key for one job.
